newsitem.title: GERMANY: VW light truck sales up but heavy truck sales weak.
newsitem.headline: VW light truck sales up but heavy truck sales weak.

text.p: Germany's Volkswagen AG said on Thursday that its 1996 west European commercial vehicle sales through August rose 13 percent to 112,000 units, raising its market share to 11.8 percent from 11.1 percent.
VW, which is Europe's largest carmaker, said the gains were due to the introduction of new truck models as VW's sales gains outpaced overall European market growth of four percent.

Bernd Wiedmann, chief executive of Volkswagen's commercial truck unit, said at the IAA truck exhibition that VW domestic truck sales through August rose despite a drop of two percent in domestic sales of vehicles weighing up to six tonnes.

"Our target for this year and the coming years is to maintain and extend our market leadership in Europe," he said. "In addition, we shall be working actively to build up our position in the new markets of central and eastern Europe."
He said the Wolfsburg-based carmaker had 31.3 percent of the German light commercial truck market through August compared with 29.6 percent in the year-ago period.

Wiedmann said he expected sales at the VW commercial truck unit, now structured as a separate brand within the VW group along with Audi, VW passenger cars, SEAT and Skoda, in 1996 to total about 10.5 billion to 11 billion marks ($7.3 billion).

He also expected VW European commercial vehicle production to total about 205,000 units compared with 155,000 in 1995 and for VW's European truck sales in 1996 to reach 6.7 billion marks compared with 5.9 billion marks in 1995.
But Wiedmann said VW was not pleased with its performance in the large truck segment where VW sells its LT delivery trucks and L80 heavy truck platform vehicles.
The first-generation LT delivery van achieved a market share of four percent in its final year of production, a figure he said was "totally unsatisfactory from our point of view".

"We have set for ourselves an extremely ambitious target with the new LT," he said, adding VW wants to sell at least 40,000 of the vehicles in 1997 and 1998 for a market share of about 10 percent in Europe for the 2.8 to 5.6 tonne class.
The new LT van was launched in June and the entire new product line will be available by the start of 1997, he said.

In eastern and central Europe, Wiedmann said VW was "yielding positive results" following an increase in production capacity at a plant in Poznan, Poland, which led to a 22 percent increase of deliveries to customers.
In Asian markets, Wiedmann said total VW commercial vehicle deliveries rose 55 percent in the first eight months of 1996.
In the North and South American markets, Wiedmann said deliveries of VW light commercial vehicles, trucks and busses topped 200,000 vehicles so far in 1996, about nine percent above year-ago levels.
VW said it estimated the worldwide commercial vehicle market at about 15.5 million vehicles, of which 13.6 million have a gross weight of up to six tonnes.
Wiedmann said the light commercial vehicle market was "an area that is growing out of proportion to the passenger car market" and would reach 18.1 million vehicles by the year 2000.
VW said its Caddy city delivery van, in its first sales year, controls 20 percent of the commercial vehicle market in Europe and about 19,000 units have been delivered.
For its larger Transporter, Caravelle and Multivan products, he said VW has a 28 percent market share in Europe following a thorough model revision at the start of 1996.
